sense: to a higher court or authority

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation; intransitive, ad + accusative of the court
evidence: Cic. Phil. 1.21 (Lewis & Short): ut dē majestāte damnātī ad populum prōvocent
terms.comment: The Roman citizen’s appeal to the people against a magistrate, and so any appeal to a higher judge: ad populum prōvocāre. Its first sense is to call out, and to challenge (to a fight, a contest); Lewis & Short.

evidence: Cic. Leg. 3.6 (Lewis & Short): ad populum prōvocātiō estō
Liv. 3.55 (Lewis & Short): est prōvocātiō, an appeal lies
terms.comment: After Augustus also a challenge to single combat; in Christian Latin a spur or encouragement (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation; the magistrate appealed to in the accusative
evidence: Cic. Quinct. 64 (Lewis & Short): ā praetōre tribūnōs appellāre
terms.comment: To call on a magistrate, classically the tribunes, for help against another; the noun is appellātiō (appellātiō prōvocātiōque, Liv. 3.56). Its everyday senses are to address and to name (see address).

evidence: Lewis & Short s.v. appellātiō II: an appeal

sources: Lewis & Short: provoco · Lewis & Short: provocatio · Lewis & Short: appello · Lewis & Short: appellatio
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 193–194, 272, 298.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
